headline: AI agent's worst bug was its own progress report, not a stall
summary: A startup analyzed every message from its first six users, finding that the AI agent's perceived failures were often due to inaccurate reporting of its own actions.
details: A startup building a cloud AI coding agent analyzed the interactions of its first six users over 21 days. They discovered that the AI agent's perceived failures, such as stalling or producing no output, were often due to internal reporting bugs rather than actual system failures.

One critical bug involved the agent's progress report, which failed to count file reads and searches. This led to instances where the agent performed significant work but reported 'nothing happened,' causing users to abandon the session.

The team found that their evaluation harness was also flawed, scoring high on trajectory quality while failing acceptance checks. This led them to incorrectly believe the agent was underperforming when the measurement tool itself was the issue.

The article emphasizes the importance of accurate instrumentation, stating, 'Check what your instrument counts before you conclude the model is bad at its job.' They learned to distinguish between the agent genuinely doing nothing and the agent investigating and stopping.

A positive finding was that one user, after receiving a well-handled token budget exhaustion message, returned the next day because the work the agent had started was worth continuing. This user also experienced the agent unprompted fixing a Next.js breakage.

The startup has since fixed the reporting bugs and improved the agent's ability to differentiate between genuine inaction and investigated stops. When the fault lies with the product, it now explicitly states it, avoiding user confusion.
caption:
We read every message our first six users sent. The worst bug was our own progress report.

A startup building a cloud AI coding agent analyzed the interactions of its first six users over 21 days. They discovered that the AI agent's perceived failures, such as stalling or producing no output, were often due to internal reporting bugs rather than actual system failures.

One critical bug involved the agent's progress report, which failed to count file reads and searches. This led to instances where the agent performed significant work but reported 'nothing happened,' causing users to abandon the session.

The team found that their evaluation harness was also flawed, scoring high on trajectory quality while failing acceptance checks. This led them to incorrectly believe the agent was underperforming when the measurement tool itself was the issue.

The article emphasizes the importance of accurate instrumentation, stating, 'Check what your instrument counts before you conclude the model is bad at its job.' They learned to distinguish between the agent genuinely doing nothing and the agent investigating and stopping.

A positive finding was that one user, after receiving a well-handled token budget exhaustion message, returned the next day because the work the agent had started was worth continuing. This user also experienced the agent unprompted fixing a Next.js breakage.

The startup has since fixed the reporting bugs and improved the agent's ability to differentiate between genuine inaction and investigated stops. When the fault lies with the product, it now explicitly states it, avoiding user confusion.
